newsitem.title: USA: Clinton cabinet reshuffle fits historical pattern.
newsitem.headline: Clinton cabinet reshuffle fits historical pattern.

text.p: In overhauling his Cabinet, President Bill Clinton has followed the pattern of second-term presidents by allowing tired officials to leave while nudging out others to reshape the government to his liking.

With the election barely won, officials began a flood of leaks to announce the impending departures, including Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Defence Secretary William Perry and Chief of Staff Leon Panetta.

Historians say the changes are typical of second-term presidencies, as fatigue takes its toll on some officials while others fall prey to their own failings, or to the president's desire for new blood.

"This is not unusual. This is what tends to happen in second terms," said Brookings Institution scholar Stephen Hess. "These are, if not killing jobs, they are certainly high energy jobs. Many Cabinet officers are not young."

That description certainly applies to Christopher, 71, who, after flying more than 700,000 miles (1.1 million km) in the president's service, became the first to formally announce his resignation at a White House ceremony on Thursday.
It also fits Perry, 69, a respected defence secretary who has travelled the globe at the president's behest.
In addition to Panetta, Christopher and Perry, officials said Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary are both expected to resign.
Former Presidents Ronald Reagan and Richard Nixon both made significant changes in their administrations on winning re-election, particularly in the top Cabinet positions.

Of the top five jobs -- chief of staff, the secretaries of state, defence and treasury and the attorney general -- four were changed on Nixon's re-election and three at the start of Reagan's second term, although this included Chief of Staff James Baker and Treasury Secretary Don Regan switching jobs.

"This is a great opportunity for a president ... to bring in new blood, with diferent skills, and to replace those people who have not worked out but whom he could not fire," said Georgetown University professor Stephen Wayne.
University of New Orleans Professor Douglas Brinkley said most top officials, if they want to leave, do so quickly so it does not seem that they wanted to stay but were forced out.
Others, who have incurred the president's wrath for one reason or another, may find it expedient to announce their reluctant resignation before they get a shove.
Although there has been some speculation Clinton aides may be eager to leave because of the scandals that may dog the president in a second term, several historians dismissed this.

"This is pretty much typical Washington ... The difference is that because the president has a number of scandals hanging over him, it leads to a certain kind of speculation that everybody's leaving before the indictments," said Brinkley.
"I think that is erroneous," he added. "You may get that from some Clinton detractors, but it just is not the case."

Clinton, whose re-election victory was tempered by the fact that voters left both houses of Congress in the hands of the Republicans, hinted broadly on Thursday that he was looking for Republicans to fill out the Cabinet.

"The American people sent us another message on Tuesday -- they want us to work together. They like it when we try to have principled compromise," Clinton said in answer to a question on who may replace Christopher. "With all these places where we have vacancies, I want to cast a wide net."

Scholars were divided on the merits of naming a member of the opposing party to the Cabinet, saying it had served past presidents well, as when Franklin Delano Roosevelt tapped Republican Henry Stimson as Secretary of War at the start of World War Two, but may be less useful to Clinton.

"It may ... help to reduce the highly partisan atmosphere on the Hill," said Georgetown's Wayne, adding: "You can't just appoint a Republican to your Cabinet and assume its done, but it's a step in the right direction."
